opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's become a pretty big part of how I work day to day. I'd say the most useful thing for me is using LLMs to build small, throwaway or semi-permanent tools that I probably wouldn't have bothered writing before because the effort-to-payoff ratio just wasn't there.

For example, I write a lot, between the books, the newsletter, and the coding notebooks, and there are all these little friction points. Things like converting formats, checking that code snippets in a manuscript actually match the code in the repository, reorganizing figures, or quickly scraping together a script that batch-processes some files. Before, I'd think, "Okay, this would take me an hour or two to write properly," and I'd just do it manually instead. Now I can describe what I want, get a first draft of the script in a minute, look it over, tweak it, and I'm done. So the barrier to automating small things has dropped a lot.

I also use them as a kind of rubber duck. When I'm implementing something from scratch, say a new attention variant or some training trick from a paper, I'll often ask the model to explain a detail or sanity-check my reasoning. I don't blindly trust the answer, but it's very good at pointing out something I might have overlooked, or at least giving me a different angle to think about.

That said, I'm still fairly hands-on. For the core code, especially the educational code where every line matters because people learn from it, I write and review it very carefully myself. The LLM helps with the scaffolding and the boring parts, but I want to understand everything that goes in. I think that's the sweet spot for me right now: let the model handle the tedious glue work so I can spend more of my time on the parts that actually require thinking.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a great question, and I think it's actually one of the areas where I've seen the biggest practical change in my own day-to-day work. I'm a big believer in small, custom tools, and historically the barrier was always that writing a little script or a utility for a one-off problem often took longer than just doing the thing manually. LLMs have really lowered that barrier for me.

A concrete example: I write a lot, both for my books and for my newsletter, and I have a whole set of little helper scripts around that workflow now. Things like checking for inconsistencies in how I format code blocks across chapters, or finding places where I use a term before I've defined it, or converting between Markdown flavors because different platforms handle them slightly differently. None of these are hard problems, but each one is annoying enough that in the past I would have just put up with it. Now I can describe what I want, get a working first version in a few minutes, and then refine it.

Another one is dealing with PDFs and research papers. I read a lot of papers, and I have scripts that help me extract and organize notes, pull out figures, that kind of thing. Again, this is tedious glue code, and I don't want to spend my mental energy on parsing edge cases in PDF libraries.

Where I'm more careful is the actual core technical work, like implementing a model architecture from scratch for a book chapter. There I still want to write the code myself, partly because the point is understanding every line, and partly because I've found LLMs are good at producing something that looks plausible and runs, but might have subtle issues, like a mismatch in how attention masks are applied or a tensor dimension that happens to broadcast correctly but for the wrong reason. So for that kind of work I use them more as a sparring partner. I'll ask, "here's my implementation, do you see anything off?" or "what's a cleaner way to express this?" rather than having them generate it for me.

And then there's the whole category of just explaining things. If I'm reading a paper and there's a notation I'm not familiar with, or I want a quick refresher on something I haven't touched in a while, that back-and-forth is really valuable. It's not that I trust the answer blindly, but it gets me unstuck faster, and I can go verify afterward.

So overall I'd say the way I think about it is: LLMs are great at removing friction from the parts of my workflow I didn't want to be doing anyway, and that frees up more time for the parts I actually care about, which for me is understanding how these models work at a fundamental level.

astra-6.text:
For me, one of the most useful things is building little tools that I probably wouldn’t have bothered building otherwise. There’s always this trade-off: I have a repetitive task, and I could automate it, but writing the automation might take longer than just doing it manually. With an LLM, that threshold gets much lower.

For example, say I need a small script to process some files or reformat some text. I can describe what I want, get a first version, and then iterate on it. I still check the code and test whether it does what I intended, but I don’t have to start from a blank page.

And I think that’s an interesting part of the value: it’s not just helping me write code faster. It makes it practical to create something very specific to my own workflow, even if I’m the only person who will ever use it.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, a lot of the value is in those little tasks where I know what I want to do, but implementing it manually would take enough time that I might put it off. Maybe I need a script to reformat some data or automate a repetitive step. I can describe what I need, get a first version, and then inspect it and iterate.

The useful part is that it lowers the effort required to build a tool for yourself. Something doesn’t have to be a big software project to be worth automating. And if it’s a workflow I use repeatedly, I’d rather turn that into a small, reliable script than keep asking the model to do the same thing every time. The LLM helps me build it, but then I can test it and run it directly.
